system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING

PHYSICS CHECK — governing physical relation is Fick's law of diffusion for ion migration (J = -D∇C), where J is flux, D is diffusion coefficient, and C is concentration. The design must reduce sodium ion diffusion coefficient D by at least 10× to meet the 0.5% annual power loss constraint under 1000 V bias at elevated temperatures (60-85°C). CALCULATED: Current modules show ~1% annual loss at these conditions; target D reduction must be significant.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — (1) Apply a sodium-blocking coating to the cover glass using atomic layer deposition (ALD) of Al2O3 or TiO2 (off-the-shelf ALD systems). (2) Modify glass manufacturing to include a sodium-diffusion barrier layer during float glass production (developed process). (3) Implement a quality control step with secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) to verify coating uniformity and sodium blocking effectiveness (off-the-shelf instrument). Procedure: Apply 20nm ALD coating to cover glass side facing cells, followed by standard module lamination.

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Implementation burden is moderate: ALD coating adds ~$0.10-0.15/W to module cost vs. standard practice, with slightly more complex manufacturing but no change in installation or maintenance. Standard practice relies on encapsulant barrier properties alone; this approach adds an active barrier at the source (glass), justifying the cost premium for high-voltage applications where PID is a dominant failure mode.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Subject 10 test modules (5 coated, 5 control) to 1000 V bias at 85°C/85% RH for 1000 hours. Measure power output before and after testing. Instruments: calibrated solar simulator, environmental chamber, high-voltage DC supply. Threshold: Coated modules must show <0.5% power loss while control modules show >2% loss. Pass/fail: All coated modules must meet threshold; if any coated module exceeds 0.5% loss, design fails. Duration: 1000 hours (accelerated test representing ~6-12 years of field conditions).
